Distinguish search failure from support failure using a bipartite graph: intervention slots on one side, admissible replacements on the other; edges encode every existing plausibility constraint. Compare greedy retention with exact maximum-cardinality matching, then minimize replacement distance at that cardinality. A larger optimum diagnoses greedy failure; isolated vertices indicate no admissible candidates, while Hall-deficient subsets reveal competition for scarce candidates under reuse limits. These are feasibility statements conditional on the candidate pool and constraints. [SciPy matching documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-1.14.1/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.csgraph.maximum_bipartite_matching.html), [Hall’s theorem](https://math.mit.edu/~goemans/18453S17/matching-notes.pdf).

Practical adaptation: replace items in place, preserving sequence length, left padding, timestamps and untouched positions. Build admissibility from available training histories and item metadata; enforce temporal availability and prespecified similarity/caliper rules before optimization. Joint multi-position constraints require validating whole edited sequences, not merely individual edges. Unbalanced optimal transport offers a related way to leave unsupported mass unmatched; retain forbidden edges explicitly rather than allowing transport penalties to soften plausibility constraints. [Matching via unbalanced optimal transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04398).

Report per-category eligible users, users with feasible interventions, matched users, coverage, constraint failures and paired prediction changes. Zero matches means no supported estimate; one match provides a descriptive case, not a credible population estimate. Label effects as sensitivity of the trained model within the supported population—matching alone does not identify behavioral causal effects. Generalized optimal matching explicitly addresses partial identification under limited overlap; broader-population claims require stated assumptions or bounds rather than extrapolation. [Kallus, 2020](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/v21/19-120.html).
